abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the factorial structure of a questionnaire assessing moral motivation within pictorial moral conflict stories in adolescents, based on theoretical moral motivation models. The questionnaire was assessed with N = 461 adolescents ( n = 253 female, 54.88%; n = 208 male, 45.12%) with a mean age of 14.26 years ( SD = 1.79, range = 10–19 years). The instrument consists of pictorial moral conflicts, depicting hypothetical conflicts in which participants evaluate moral decisions made by others and themselves, attribute emotions to moral and immoral actions, assess their sense of duty for moral actions, and judge the admissibility of immoral actions. The scenarios in the stories systematically vary in action orientation (prohibitive vs. prosocial), type of harm (physical, social, or property-related), and group affiliation (in-group vs. out-group). Confirmatory factor analysis showed that a model including only the six correlated dimensions did not adequately represent the data. Model fit improved substantially when orthogonal scenario factors were included to account for dependencies between responses referring to the same pictorial story. Overall, the findings support a multidimensional assessment of moral motivation while highlighting the importance of accounting for scenario-specific dependencies when using pictorial moral conflicts. This study provides a tool for assessing moral motivation in adolescents, offering new insights into the interplay between cognitive, emotional, and situational factors in moral conflicts.

abstract: Post-COVID condition (PCC) affects a substantial proportion of individuals following acute COVID-19 infection, with manifestations such as dysautonomia, fatigue and brain fog. The cervicothoracic sympathetic chain block (CSB), a local anaesthetic block of the cervical sympathetic trunk, has shown preliminary promise in uncontrolled studies, but randomised evidence is lacking. This trial is expected to provide a rigorous estimate of the efficacy of CSB compared with a placebo saline injection for PCC. The CeASE randomised controlled trial (RCT) is a double-blind, parallel-group RCT enrolling 78 adult participants with PCC across two Canadian sites (Women’s College Hospital and Toronto Western Hospital). Participants will be randomised 1:1 to receive two ultrasound-guided injections of either 0.25% bupivacaine with epinephrine (active CSB) or 0.9% normal saline (placebo control), spaced 1–2 weeks apart. The primary outcome is a change in the Modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRSm) Symptom Severity subscale at 1 month following the final injection. Secondary outcomes include C19-YRSm scores at 3 months, cardiovascular autonomic function (heart rate variability, postural heart rate changes and blood pressure responses), serum proinflammatory cytokine levels (interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha), autonomic symptom burden (Composite Autonomic Symptom Score-31), mental health (Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), quality of life (EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level questionnaire, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), and actigraphy-measured sleep and physical activity. The sample size of 78 participants (39 per arm) was calculated for a target between-group difference of four points on the C19-YRSm Symptom Severity subscale, assuming an SD of 5.62, 85% power and a 10% dropout allowance. Recruitment opened in May 2026; final follow-up is expected by September 2027. Ethics approval was obtained from the University Health Network Institutional Review Board (25-6183). Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and presentation at relevant scientific conferences. Deidentified individual participant data will be shared, in accordance with the data sharing plan recorded in the trial registration, on reasonable request. abstract: Prosocial punishment, an important factor to stabilize cooperation in social dilemma games, often faces challenges like second-order free-riders-who cooperate but avoid punishing to save costs-and antisocial punishers, who defect and retaliate against cooperators. Addressing these challenges, our study introduces prosocial punishment bots that consistently cooperate and punish free-riders. Our findings reveal that these bots significantly promote the emergence of prosocial punishment among normal players due to their 'sticky effect'-an unwavering commitment to cooperation and punishment that magnetically attracts their opponents to emulate this strategy. Additionally, we observe that the prevalence of prosocial punishment is greatly enhanced when normal players exhibit a tendency to follow a 'copying the majority' strategy, or when bots are strategically placed in high-degree nodes within scale-free networks. Conversely, bots designed for defection or antisocial punishment diminish overall cooperation levels. This stark contrast underscores the critical role of strategic bot design in enhancing cooperative behaviours in human/AI interactions. Our findings open new avenues in evolutionary game theory, demonstrating the potential of human-machine collaboration in solving the conundrum of punishment.

abstract: The global ageing population trend has heightened the need to understand various factors affecting geriatric well-being, including beliefs and attitudes about death. Positive perspectives about death, such as those gained from practicing maranasati (death contemplation in Buddhism), may enhance psychological resilience and prosocial behavior, key factors promoted in public mental health. Death reflection can encourage the development of the Four Immeasurable Minds (equanimity, loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy), Buddhist virtues that promote public harmony and enhance well-being. The current study investigated whether positive beliefs and attitudes about death influenced well-being directly or indirectly through the Four Immeasurable Minds among older Thai Buddhists, contributing to culturally informed mental health strategies. Data were collected from 332 older adults in Northern Thailand. The study collected information on positive beliefs and attitudes about death using the Morana Questionnaire, well-being using the WHO-5 index (Thai), and Four Immeasurable Minds using the Four Immeasurable Inventory. The data were analyzed using mediation analysis, accounting for potential confounding variables. Positive beliefs about death had a significant and positive effect on well-being, and prosocial values mediated this relationship. The findings suggest that positive beliefs about death can promote prosocial values and contribute to a healthy sense of well-being among Buddhist Thai older adult. Integrating culturally adapted, mindfulness-based approaches into public mental health initiatives could support healthy aging, particularly in Buddhist communities. Further research should explore scalable interventions to promote psychological resilience in diverse older populations.

abstract: In this article, we argue for the potential value of participatory multi-agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) modeling for addressing the pragmatic challenge of promoting a sustainable altruism among individuals and groups that will enable us to find pathways of collective action that lead toward more peaceful coexistence. Along the way, we note that this approach to modeling also addresses the scientific challenge within computer science and social simulation of creating more psychologically realistic artificial agents whose interactions occur in more realistic social networks. We identify some of the evolved cognitive and coalitional biases that make it so difficult to achieve an equilibrium of sustainable altruism in contemporary human societies, describe some of the innovative ways in which recent advances in MAAI approaches to psychological and cultural modeling open up new opportunities for simulating solutions to these challenges, and address some of the ethical issues associated with using modeling and simulating methods to help us proactively navigate the Anthropocene.

abstract: Empathy and sympathy have been widely recognized as core antecedents of prosocial behavior. However, prior literature has treated the two constructs inconsistently, with sympathy frequently subsumed under an overly broad and ill - defined conceptualization of empathy. This conceptual overlap has limited discriminant operationalization, hindered cumulative theoretical development, and consequently constrained applied precision in interdisciplinary contexts. The present study examined whether empathy and sympathy constituted structurally distinguishable knowledge domains with divergent intellectual foundations and developmental trajectories. A comparative bibliometric analysis was conducted using SSCI-indexed articles retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection for the period 2015-2025. The dataset comprised 4,413 empathy-related publications and 247 sympathy-related publications. VOSviewer and CiteSpace were employed to perform keyword co-occurrence mapping, document co-citation clustering, burst detection, and strategic coordinate analysis. This study provided the first comparative scientometric evidence to distinguish the structural divergence between empathy and sympathy research. Results showed that empathy research formed a dense, interdisciplinary, and mature thematic structure, whereas sympathy research was relatively small, fragmented, and often subsumed under empathy-related clusters. Based on quantitative mapping and theoretical integration, we developed a four-dimensional operational indicator framework with fifteen second-order indicators. This framework translates structural knowledge patterns into a systematic conceptual reference for future measurement and modeling studies. By combining scientometric analysis with conceptual reconstruction, this study helps clarify a long-standing definitional ambiguity and provides a novel data-driven approach for differentiating overlapping constructs in social science research.

abstract: Self-conscious emotions, such as embarrassment, guilt, shame and pride, play a central role in managing reputation and interpersonal relationships. They are thought to emerge in the first years of life, with children's developing cognitive capacities and their growing appreciation of social norms and rules. Recent years have seen a rapid increase in research on self-conscious emotions in early life, supported by advanced methods including manual and automated micro-coding of non-verbal behaviour, depth sensor imaging and physiological measures. In this narrative review, we summarize this emerging evidence from developmental science, which suggests that self-conscious emotions may be observed earlier than previously thought-within the first months and years of life-and that they seem to serve both motivational and communicative functions from early on. Specifically, they motivate socially appropriate behaviours, such as helping others, while communicating adherence to social norms and rules. Further, we highlight current limitations in the field and recommend more experimental and longitudinal studies especially in infancy and toddlerhood, the integration of multi-modal data and the use of naturalistic tasks to advance our understanding of self-conscious emotions in early development. This article is part of the theme issue 'Mechanisms, development, phylogeny and functions of emotional expressions'.

abstract: This paper develops the life-sustenance hypothesis to explain the multifaceted phenomenon of the human-nature connection. It is based on an interpretation of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy brought into contemporary times via recent multidisciplinary research and theoretical underpinnings. Rousseau suggested that humans have two innate, instinctive drives he called amour-de-soi and pitié—a self-preservative drive, and its enlargement, an inclination to help other living beings in distress. The life-sustenance hypothesis is rooted in a systems biological framework situating humans as interconnected parts within a nested system of life. Corresponding to Rousseau’s drives, this interconnectedness is suggested to give rise to the dynamics between two life-preserving orientations that guide our manners-of-being in the world: a self-sustaining and a ‘life-sustaining’ orientation shared by all organisms, albeit manifested differently. The experience of nature connectedness, along with altruistic impulses, are proposed to be human manifestations of the life-sustaining orientation. Moreover, in line with Rousseau’s philosophy, it is posited that the modern, individualistic lifestyle has given rise to an imbalance between these orientations leading to problems in prosociality, proenvironmentalism, and overall well-being. One means by which to regain balanced manners-of-being might be to enhance our nature connectedness. Possible physiological indicators for the hypothesis are explored.

abstract: This scoping review maps key constructs of child flourishing, examines their conceptualization and measurement, and synthesizes their associations with developmental outcomes. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, focusing on individual-level positive psychological resources (e.g., subjective wellbeing, gratitude, hope, character strengths, resilience, and self-efficacy) and children's experiences within the Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) context with positive education. In total, 68 studies were included in the final review. Data were charted and synthesized narratively. Evidence suggests that these constructs demonstrate generally stable development across early childhood and are associated with positive outcomes, including social-emotional competence, prosocial behavior, and learning engagement. Partial support was found for the broaden-and-built theory and the undoing hypothesis. Measurement approaches varied considerably across studies, with a lack of consistent, standardized instruments and limited evidence on the developmental trajectories of these constructs. Children's experiences in ECEC, particularly character education through art, resilience projects through teamwork and mindfulness, emerged as integral to flourishing and interacted with psychological resources. Greater conceptual clarity, standardized measures, and inclusive, theory-driven research are needed to advance the field.

abstract: This methodological paper, informed by a targeted structured narrative review of contemporary nursing participatory action research studies, aims to distinguish participatory action research from participatory research and patient and public involvement and engagement, examine how participation, shared decision-making, power-sharing, iterative inquiry and collective action are operationalised, and provide practical guidance for nursing researchers across different health settings. A methodological paper informed by a targeted structured narrative review of contemporary nursing participatory action research studies. The review used predefined eligibility criteria, structured searches and duplicate screening to identify contemporary illustrative studies. Data were examined for study context, individuals with lived experience involved, methods of invitation, participatory activities, shared decision-making, iterative processes and the action developed, implemented and evaluated. PubMed and CINAHL were searched in April 2025 for nursing studies published during the preceding five years using terms for nurses or nursing combined with participatory action research, participatory research, or action research. The studies were used as contemporary illustrations and were not ranked for methodological quality. The 20 illustrative studies reported diverse approaches, but the depth of participation, shared decision-making, power-sharing and action was inconsistently described. The synthesis identifies relationship-building, explicit negotiation of power, collaborative interpretation, collectively agreed action, reflexivity and transparent reporting as central considerations in nursing participatory action research. Participatory action research can help nurses respond to patient, family and community priorities by involving individuals with lived experience in shaping decisions, interpreting findings and collective action. Although participatory action research may draw on patient and public involvement and engagement principles, it is distinguished by collaborative inquiry, negotiated power, shared decision-making, co-production of knowledge and collectively agreed action. Participatory action research can extend nursing practice beyond consultation by enabling patients, families, and communities to share authority over research priorities, interpretation and action. This paper provides practical guidance on partnership formation, power sharing, collaborative interpretation, action, methodological rigour and transparent reporting. The recommendations are linked to patterns and gaps observed across contemporary nursing studies and to core participatory action research literature. A targeted structured narrative review was used to support methodological development rather than to provide an exhaustive synthesis of the field. Reporting therefore focuses on transparent study identification and selection and the included studies are used as contemporary illustrations. This study did not include patients or the public in its design, conduct, or reporting.

abstract: Social dilemmas present a significant challenge in multi-agent cooperation because individuals are incentivised to behave in ways that undermine socially optimal outcomes. Consequently, self-interested agents often avoid collective behaviour. In response, we formalise social dilemmas and introduce a novel metric, the general self-interest level, to quantify the disparity between individual and group rationality in such scenarios. This metric represents the maximum proportion of their individual rewards that agents can retain while ensuring that a social welfare optimum becomes a dominant strategy. Our approach diverges from traditional concepts of altruism, instead focusing on strategic reward redistribution. By transferring rewards among agents in a manner that aligns individual and group incentives, rational agents will maximise collective welfare while pursuing their own interests. We provide an algorithm to compute efficient transfer structures for an arbitrary number of agents, and introduce novel multi-player social dilemma games to illustrate the effectiveness of our method. This work provides both a descriptive tool for analysing social dilemmas and a prescriptive solution for resolving them via efficient reward transfer contracts. Applications include mechanism design, where we can assess the impact on collaborative behaviour of modifications to models of environments.

abstract: Recent theories of socio-moral development assume that humans evolved a capacity to evaluate others' social actions in different kinds of interactions. Prior infant studies found both reaching and visual preferences for the prosocial over the antisocial agents. However, whether the attribution of either positive or negative valence to agents' actions involved in an aggressive chasing interaction can be inferred by both reaching behaviors and visual attention deployment (i.e., disengagement of visual attention) is still an open question. Here we presented 7-month-old infants (N = 92) with events displaying an aggressive chasing interaction. By using preferential reaching and an attentional task (i.e., overlap paradigm), we assessed whether and how infants evaluate aggressive chasing interactions. The results demonstrated that young infants prefer to reach the victim over the aggressor, but neither agent affects visual attention. Moreover, such reaching preferences emerged only when dynamic cues and emotional face-like features were congruent with agents' social roles. Overall, these findings suggested that infants' evaluations of aggressive interactions are based on infants' sensitivity to some kinematic cues that characterized agents' actions and, especially, to the congruency between such motions and the face-like emotional expressions of the agents.

abstract: As a foundation of social interaction, interpersonal coordination is boosted in prosocial contexts but undermined by negative situations. Exactly how social factors shape coordination is, however, unknown. Previous literature demonstrates that for coordination to emerge people must attend to their interaction partners. This evidence, however, draws from sterile laboratory studies employing heavy-handed manipulations of little interpersonal relevance. By contrast, in more naturalistic contexts subtle differences in how people attend to themselves and others (e.g., a lingering glance vs. a suspicious side glance) can profoundly change the course of interaction. Understanding how social factors shape interpersonal coordination therefore requires consideration of aspects of attentional behaviour that better characterise everyday interaction. To this end, the current research employed virtual reality (VR) to explore how two core features of social attention, focus (self vs. other) and partner gaze (direct vs. averted), influence the spontaneous coordination of arm and head movements. The results indicated that: (i) coordination was enhanced in the other (cf. self) focus condition; and (ii) coordination was diminished in the averted (cf. direct) gaze condition. These findings provide novel evidence to indicate that the emergence of interpersonal coordination varies as a function of the everyday attentional behaviours that punctuate naturalistic social exchange. Of broad theoretical note, here we demonstrate that the among the factors constraining interpersonal coordination, the distribution of attention between self and other plays a meaningful role.

abstract: Kind emotions (e.g. empathy for others, self-compassion and gratitude) motivate kind actions and involve understanding, appreciating or 'feeling with' both one's own and others' emotions. They are an essential capacity for humans' potential to care for fellow humans and non-human entities. How do such emotions evolve, and what type of caring environments and mechanisms are needed for their development? In this review, we provide insights into how children's kind emotions emerge, develop and are nurtured by caring environments. We begin by reviewing the development of kind emotions across the early years and identify consequences of kind emotions on prosociality and well-being. Next, we summarize research on the mechanisms and functions of caring environments in shaping the development of kind emotions, including caring relationships and practices of care across diverse relationships (e.g. with parents and peers) and layers of the ecosystem (e.g. familial, educational, societal and natural). Finally, we provide recommendations for future developmental research in this area. This article is part of the theme issue 'Mechanisms, development, phylogeny and functions of emotional expressions'.

abstract: Concevoir des esprits sociaux : Comment le design de l'IA et les normes de communication façonnent la perception, l'engagement et le comportement prosocial des humains L'importance des agents conversationnels numériques a récemment augmenté, de nombreuses entreprises adoptant des agents pilotés par l'IA pour gérer les demandes d'affaires et faciliter les interactions quotidiennes avec les clients. Étant donné la réticence générale des individus envers l'IA, certaines entreprises choisissent d'anthropomorphiser leurs bots de service client (par exemple, en leur donnant des noms et des avatars). Cependant, l'efficacité de ces pratiques n'est pas claire dans le cas des voicebots (c'est-à-dire, des bots conversationnels basés sur la voix), car ces interventions ne sont pas axées sur la voix. Nous nous concentrons sur la voix, en tant que caractéristique clé des voicebots, et proposons une approche d'anthropomorphisme axée sur la voix. À travers une série de cinq expériences, nous démontrons le rôle de l'attribution d'un accent au voicebot sur les perceptions anthropomorphiques et l'engagement ultérieur des utilisateurs. Plus précisément, nous montrons que les utilisateurs ont une préférence plus marquée pour interagir avec des voicebots et adoptent des attitudes plus positives envers eux lorsque ces voicebots sont équipés d'accents étrangers. Nous mettons en lumière le rôle sous-jacent des perceptions anthropomorphiques en tant que mécanisme psychologique, suggérant que les accents étrangers servent de cue anthropomorphique crucial, influençant l'attitude des utilisateurs et entraînant une préférence pour les voicebots par rapport aux agents en direct. Ces résultats fournissent des éclairages pour les entreprises cherchant à améliorer l'engagement client grâce à leur voicebot, ainsi que pour les entreprises impliquées dans le développement des technologies voicebot

abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain malignancy in adults. Despite the Stupp protocol, median overall survival remains approximately 15 months, and the inadequacy of current therapies combined with the restrictive permeability of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) underscore the need for new therapeutic candidates. This study aimed to evaluate the sequence isomeric dipeptides H-tryptophan-glutamic acid-OH (H-Trp-Glu-OH) and H-glutamic acid-tryptophan-OH (H-Glu-Trp-OH), hereafter abbreviated Trp-Glu and Glu-Trp, as potential anticancer agents against GBM through an integrated computational and experimental approach. Geometry optimization and electronic structure analyses were performed in Gaussian at the B3LYP/6-311 ++G(d,p) level. A conformational search over multiple starting geometries preceded optimization, and vibrational frequency calculations confirmed that all reported structures are true minima. Two reference states were used, each applied identically to both sequence isomers so that every comparison is strictly like-for-like. The electronic structure calculations and the ADMET predictions were carried out on the neutral form, which is the interpretable reference state for Koopmans-based reactivity descriptors and the input convention of the ADMET predictor; molecular docking and molecular dynamics were carried out on the anionic species that predominates at pH 7.4 (NH3 +, two COO-; net charge -1), which is the species that actually engages the binding sites. Molecular docking against six GBM-associated target proteins (CHI3L1-YKL-40/8R41, PI3K-alpha/4JPS, VEGFR-2/4ASD, IDH1 R132H/4UMX, STAT3/6NJS, and System xc-/7P9U) was performed using AutoDock Vina with grid-box centres, box dimensions, exhaustiveness, pose count and random seed reported in full; the protocol was validated by redocking each co-crystallized ligand into its own site and computing the heavy-atom RMSD against the crystallographic pose. Three targets (CHI3L1/YKL-40, VEGFR-2 and IDH1 R132H) were carried forward to 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in Schrodinger Desmond using the OPLS4 force field, one trajectory per complex, with both sequence isomers built in the same ionization state. Every docking calculation was repeated with five independent random seeds and is reported as mean +/- SD; the redocking validation was performed as a single run per target. No MM-GBSA binding free-energy estimation with per-residue decomposition. Comprehensive ADMET profiling was carried out using ADMETlab 3.0. In vitro anticancer activity was evaluated in U-87 GBM cells using the MTT assay at 10-100 μg/mL over 24, 48, and 72 h, with temozolomide as the reference agent; all concentrations are reported in both mass and molar units, and 72 h IC50 values with 95% confidence intervals were obtained by non-linear regression. In the corrected screen, every docking calculation was repeated with five independent random seeds and scores are reported as mean +/- SD. Glu-Trp gave the strongest score of the panel against CHI3L1/YKL-40 (8R41, -8.60 +/- 0.05 kcal/mol). Trp-Glu scored highest against CHI3L1/YKL-40 and VEGFR-2 (-8.19 +/- 0.24 and -8.17 +/- 0.02 kcal/mol), two values that are indistinguishable from one another. The two isomers ranked the six targets almost identically, but the difference between them lay within the seed-to-seed variability of the scoring function at only one of the six targets (System xc-, 0.08 +/- 0.21 kcal/mol); at the remaining five the separation exceeded that variability. VEGFR-2 was the exception of mechanistic interest: there the isomers occupied two distinct sub-pockets, Trp-Glu at the ATP-site hinge and Glu-Trp in the type-II back pocket, sharing no contact residue. Redocking of the co-crystallized ligand reproduced the crystallographic pose within the conventional 2.0 Å criterion for four of the six targets (VEGFR-2 0.54 Å, PI3K-alpha 0.62 Å, CHI3L1 1.02 Å, IDH1 R132H 1.20 Å), with STAT3 at 2.65 Å and System xc- at 3.91 Å. The HOMO-LUMO energy gap was 4.818 eV for Trp-Glu and 4.952 eV for Glu-Trp, a difference of 0.134 eV that is too small to be treated as evidence of differing biological activity. Molecular dynamics was extended from one target to three and each complex was simulated for 100 ns with both isomers in the same ionization state. The two sequences behaved differently, and in opposite directions at different targets. At VEGFR-2 Glu-Trp held its docked pose, with ligand RMSD confined to roughly 2-3.5 Å and hydrogen bonds to Glu885 and Arg1027 persisting for most of the trajectory, whereas Trp-Glu left its starting pose within the first 20 ns and settled into an alternative surface site anchored by Arg929 and Arg932. At IDH1 R132H the ordering reversed: Trp-Glu showed the smaller positional drift and a persistent hydrogen-bond network centred on Ile128, Ser287 and Ala282. At CHI3L1/YKL-40 Trp-Glu also relaxed out of its initial pose after approximately 65-70 ns; the Glu-Trp ligand of that system had been built without explicit bond-order information, so the Glu-Trp results at this target are reported as provisional and the comparison between the isomers there is not treated as quantitative. Each complex was simulated once rather than in replicate, and MM-GBSA free energies were not computed. ADMET profiling returned a mixed rather than a uniformly favourable picture: low predicted hERG and AMES liabilities, but one Lipinski violation (six hydrogen-bond donors), poor predicted Caco-2 and MDCK permeability, poor human liver microsome stability, very low predicted BBB permeability, and elevated nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and genotoxicity probabilities. In the MTT assay, both dipeptides exerted negligible cytotoxicity at 24-48 h but produced marked, significant reductions in viability at 72 h. Trp-Glu displayed a monotonic concentration-response with its strongest effect at the highest concentration tested (100 μg/mL, 300 μM; IC50 82.9 μg/mL), whereas Glu-Trp displayed a non-monotonic concentration-response with its strongest effect at the lowest concentration tested (10 μg/mL, 30 μM). Because temozolomide was included as a single-concentration reference (100 μM, equivalent to 19.4 μg/mL) rather than as part of a dose-response series, the comparison is presented on a molar basis and no claim of superiority over temozolomide is made. Because Trp-Glu and Glu-Trp are sequence isomers of identical molecular formula and identical ionizable groups, every difference observed between them is attributable to residue order and to nothing else. On that controlled comparison the study makes one substantive finding, supported independently by two methods: sequence directionality changes where and how these dipeptides engage a protein. In docking it relocated the ligand between two distinct sub-pockets of VEGFR-2 with no contact residue in common, and in molecular dynamics it determined which isomer retained its initial pose, with the advantage reversing between VEGFR-2 and IDH1 R132H. The same directionality is visible in the cells, where the two isomers produced opposite concentration-response patterns at 72 h. The present work does not establish blood-brain barrier penetration, target engagement, mechanism of action or in vivo efficacy; the very low predicted BBB permeability and several elevated in silico toxicity flags are substantial liabilities. These dipeptides are therefore best regarded as starting structures whose sequence-dependent behaviour merits further mechanistic investigation, rather than as candidates ready for preclinical development.

abstract: Social enterprises combine social purpose and commercial activity to address societal challenges, yet limited longitudinal evidence explains how they develop as they expand, particularly when operating within established institutions. This study examines the factors supporting expansion in a university-based social enterprise and how their function and importance change across stages of development. We conduct a 15-year longitudinal case study of an enterprise delivering substance use prevention to secondary school students through face-to-face and digital formats. Evidence includes trial and survey data, organizational records, governance and funding documentation, and an extensive body of peer-reviewed publications. Using a social innovation lens, the study examines the roles of university actors, schools, government, funders and industry across the expansion process. Expansion was accompanied by increasing interdependence between the enterprise and the university. The university provided credibility, expertise, resources and institutional support, while the enterprise contributed to the university's research activity and social mission. Technology also changed how work was coordinated as the organization developed. Initially embedded in the program offering, digital systems increasingly supported communication, collaboration, implementation monitoring and knowledge sharing across staff, schools, university actors and external stakeholders. As the enterprise expanded, roles and implementation processes became more structured, alongside greater requirements for technological oversight, security and accountability. This was important for replicability as the program introduced new platforms and expanded nationally. These findings show that social enterprise expansion involves reconfiguring the organizational systems and relationships through which social value is produced. The longitudinal perspective provides contextual and practical detail on how to achieve this for social enterprises working in a university setting.

abstract: Extensive juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JORRP) can turn the paediatric airway into a constantly changing operative field, particularly when disease extends from the larynx into the tracheobronchial tree. Shared airway surgery, the risk of obstruction and the dynamic changes that occur during lesion excision make anaesthetic management especially challenging. We describe the anaesthetic management of a two-year-old child with extensive laryngotracheobronchial papillomatosis and a long-term tracheostomy after failed decannulation. A staged airway strategy was used, with spontaneous ventilation preserved throughout. At induction, the existing metallic tracheostomy tube was exchanged for a cuffed flexometallic endotracheal tube. After lesion debulking, a significant air leak developed, so the tube was changed to a microlaryngeal surgery (MLS) tube to improve the tracheal seal while maintaining surgical access. For excision of distal airway lesions, the MLS tube was removed, and tubeless oxygenation was provided with transnasal humidified rapid-insufflation ventilatory exchange (THRIVE). The procedure was completed successfully, and the tracheostomy tube was reinserted at the end. Intraoperative challenges included airway sharing, significant airway leak, and laryngospasm, all of which were managed successfully. Successful management requires anticipation of dynamic airway changes and the ability to transition between different ventilation strategies.

abstract: Patients with multimorbidity, multisystem disease, rare conditions, or competing treatment priorities frequently require coordination beyond the scope of a single specialty. This Project Report describes the development and implementation of a hospital-wide multidisciplinary team (MDT) care model at a tertiary general hospital in China. The report synthesizes institutional documents and routine program records describing MDT governance, workflow, digital support, operational activity, and implementation experience. Quantitative indicators for 2021-2025 were summarized descriptively. No comparator group was included, and no causal effectiveness analysis or inferential statistical testing was performed. Initiated with a geriatric medicine MDT in 2015, the program subsequently developed into a hospital-wide framework comprising seven clinical-domain-based MDT centers by 2023. The number of participating departments increased from 4 in 2021 to 23 in 2025, while the annual number of patients receiving MDT care increased overall from 32 to 223. Virtual MDT predominated during 2021-2022, whereas on-site MDT became the predominant mode from 2023 onward. MDT sessions involving trainees increased from 15 in 2021 to 119 in 2025. The program incorporated standardized case selection, structured multidisciplinary review, documented consensus planning, follow-up and repeat review, and digital support for information sharing and remote participation. Implementation experience highlighted practical challenges related to expert coordination, multidisciplinary consensus, information completeness, follow-up, clinician participation, and cross-campus coordination. The experience indicates that hospital-wide MDT care functions as an institutional coordination system rather than an isolated case-conference mechanism. Implementation of such a model may depend on governance, standardized workflows, reliable information exchange, administrative coordination, clinician participation, and closed-loop follow-up. Prospective evaluation is required to determine effects on clinical, process, patient-reported, and economic outcomes.

abstract: Long COVID is a multisystemic condition characterized by persistent symptoms after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, whose biological mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Host genetic factors may be associated, and the sharing of genetic architecture with other chronic diseases such as viral hepatitis B and C may aid in understanding this disease. A cross-sectional study was conducted including 150 individuals stratified into two groups: (i) Long COVID and (ii) chronic viral hepatitis B and C. Eighteen single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) previously associated with COVID-19 severity and inflammatory pathways were genotyped using TaqMan® real-time PCR assays. The analyses of genetic association models were performed using multivariate logistic regression adjusted for gender, self-reported skin color, and comorbidities. Mental health scales for assessing depression (Beck), anxiety (Hamilton), fatigue, and post-COVID functional scale were used both to define the syndrome and for subsequent analyses of the genotypic profile probably associated with Long COVID. Among all the SNPs analyzed, rs12610495 (A/G) in the DPP9 gene was the only variant consistently associated with Long COVID. After adjustment for sex, self-reported skin color, and hepatitis status, carriers of the G variant allele demonstrated increased odds of Long COVID under the dominant model (OR = 2.66; 95% CI: 1.08-6.57; p = 0.029) and the overdominant model (OR = 2.96; 95% CI: 1.17-7.52; p = 0.018). The association was more pronounced in women (OR = 3.30; 95% CI: 1.08-10.07). Exploratory analyses of mental and functional outcomes did not reach statistical significance, although a higher frequency of functional limitation and fatigue was observed among carriers of the G allele. This study suggests that DPP9 rs12610495 is associated with Long COVID, previously associated only with severe acute COVID, demonstrating that individuals carrying the rs12610495 G variant allele had higher odds of developing Long COVID. The inclusion of viral hepatitis as a chronic inflammatory condition for comparison contributed to the identification of shared genetic archetypal among diseases, revealing the possible role of DPP9 with Long COVID and highlighting this gene as a relevant target for future validation studies.

abstract: Quantifying protein-protein binding affinity is essential for understanding molecular recognition and guiding antibody and inhibitor design. However, binding affinity is governed by tightly coupled sequence, structural, and chemical determinants. Existing models often encode these factors in isolation, limiting their ability to capture the multi-level dependencies underlying binding affinity [Formula: see text]. We propose MIRAGE, a graph-based framework for direct [Formula: see text] prediction that explicitly models interactions across multidimensional (1D sequences, 2D contact maps, 3D structures) and multi-scale (residue-level, atom-level) features. MIRAGE integrates two complementary modules to capture cross-dimensional and cross-scale dependencies, enabling unified residue-atom representation learning. Across public benchmarks, MIRAGE demonstrated strong generalization, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.70 and 0.69 on two independent external test sets and retaining predictive effectiveness under structure-separated cross-validation designed to reduce structural information sharing. In a supplementary analysis with AlphaFold3-predicted complex structures, MIRAGE also preserved significant predictive correlations when experimentally resolved structures were unavailable. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of each module. Interpretability analyses further show that the model focuses on biophysically meaningful interface regions. The source code of MIRAGE is available from https://github.com/ShiweiWu-545/MIRAGE . These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-level interactions is important for accurately capturing the determinants of binding affinity. MIRAGE provides an interpretable and robust framework for structure-aware [Formula: see text] prediction, with potential applications in protein engineering and drug design.

abstract: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic shown to have enduring antidepressant effects. Currently, the mechanism for its enduring effects is not well understood. abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

abstract: Dichos (sayings) and moralejas (stories with moral lessons) are important cultural traditions within Latine families that transmit values, knowledge, and life lessons across generations. While previous research has examined their use in educational settings and parenting programs, less is known about their long-term influence on the experiences of Latine adults. Guided by the Intergenerational Transmission of Cultural Socialization framework, this study explored (1) what dichos and moralejas Latine adults learned from their caregivers and (2) how dichos and moralejas support their current experiences as adults. Twenty Latine adults participated in semi-structured interviews conducted in English or Spanish. An inductive thematic analysis identified 72 dichos and moralejas participants learned from caregivers organized into seven categories: (a) work, effort, and perseverance; (b) character, conduct, and life lessons; (c) family, relationships, and identity; (d) caution, safety, and social behavior; (e) gratitude, humility, and generosity; (f) home and community interactions; and (g) time, opportunity, and fate. Participants described these teachings as shaping their work ethic, resilience, moral decision-making, social relationships, and family identity, while also providing examples of continued intergenerational transmission. Participants reported that the developmental impact of the dichos and moralejas increased when their meanings became clearer with the accumulation of life experiences. Findings highlight the role of dichos and moralejas as enduring cultural resources that support resilience, identity, and intergenerational continuity among Latine communities.

abstract: We study the wellbeing returns from volunteering in England's National Health Service (NHS) Volunteer Responders, set up in response to Covid-19. Using linked survey and administrative data, we exploit the oversubscription of volunteers and the random allocation of tasks via an app to establish causality. Volunteers show stronger wellbeing and feelings of belongingness and connectedness to their local area. Welfare analyses suggest that the benefits of the program substantially exceeded its costs. We are the first to study the welfare effects of a nationwide volunteering program. Our findings show that prosocial behavor improves personal wellbeing as well as social welfare.

abstract: Admission of a child to a paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) is highly distressing for caregivers, who face uncertainty about the child's outcome and disruption of normal caregiving roles. In low-resource settings such as Malawi, where psychosocial support is limited, little is known about caregivers' experiences during their child's PICU admission. This study explored psychosocial experiences, coping mechanisms and support needs of caregivers of children admitted to Mercy James PICU in Malawi. A qualitative exploratory-descriptive study was conducted between October and December 2024 at Mercy James PICU within Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Blantyre. Eleven caregivers of children admitted for over 48 h were purposively sampled for in-depth, semi-structured interviews, which were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated and analysed thematically. The transactional theory of stress and coping guided interpretation of findings. Four themes were identified: emotional and psychological distress, caregivers' perceptions of care delivery, coping mechanisms and perceived support needs. Caregivers experienced both immediate and ongoing distress associated with sudden PICU admission, uncertainty, separation from family and financial strain. Perceptions of care were shaped by interactions with staff and hospital environment. Caregivers used both problem-focused strategies, like information seeking, and emotion-focused strategies like reliance on God, social support and acceptance. They reported unmet needs for psychological support, compassionate care and access to food. Caregivers of children in PICU experience significant psychosocial challenges shaped by admission context, environment and limited support. Strengthening communication and information-sharing practices, compassionate care, structured emotional support and addressing basic needs is essential.

abstract: Music has existed in human culture for at least 40,000 years and is present today in all societies. Its perception, appreciation and production are based on a set of cognitive abilities commonly referred to as "musicality." Some authors have suggested that musicality may have an evolutionary origin. Specifically, it may have evolved because music promotes social cohesion within groups. This hypothesis is supported by studies in developmental psychology, which show that joint music-making promotes empathy in 8 to 11-year-olds, as well as cooperation and helping behavior in 4-year-old children. However, many questions remain unanswered, particularly regarding the effects of music listening on social behavior (beyond joint production), the conditions under which such effects may be observed (e.g., individual versus joint listening), the musical properties and mechanisms involved (e.g., the role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization), and the broader evolution of musicality across the living world beyond our own species. In 2017, we already demonstrated a positive influence of joint listening to classical music on social interaction in a cooperative task context in children aged 3 to 6, as well as in a parrot species, the cockatiels (suggesting convergent evolution in humans and certain birds, thus indicating a partly biological, not just cultural, origin of musicality). The study presented here focuses specifically on children but is also part of a larger comparative project involving humans, non-human primates, and birds. In the case of children, this study showed that percussive, rhythmic electronic music fostered more social interactions and cooperation among pairs of 3 to 6-year-old children compared to classical music (Mozart's Sonata K448), white noise, a "scrambled" version of the stimulus used, or silence. The role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization will be further explored in the future by testing the influence of new stimuli listened to together or separately, with or without concurrent music production. We also plan to examine the spontaneous movements of individuals during listening and their relationship to observed behaviors in subsequent prosocial tasks.

abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. We tested 113 English-speaking children aged 8-10 years from a UK primary school. Analyses showed that reading and prosocial behaviour are related, and that the relation was partly explained by variance shared with empathy, particularly affective rather than cognitive empathy. Future work focusing on causal aspects of these relations should provide further guidance on the practical implications of these results.

abstract: Adolescent major depressive disorder (MDD) is heterogeneous, with diverse and frequently co-occurring psychopathological manifestations. Family-related experiences, childhood trauma, rumination, and psychological resilience are linked to adolescent mental health, but whether their associations differ across clinical domains remains unclear. This cross-sectional study included 80 adolescents with MDD and 53 healthy controls. Family functioning, parenting, childhood trauma, rumination, psychological resilience, and four clinical domains comprising affective distress, suicidal ideation, the non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) spectrum, and self-regulation difficulties were assessed using validated instruments. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) examined multivariate associations across the combined control + MDD sample, reflecting the dimensional continuum of adolescent psychopathology. MDD-only analyses examined associations within the diagnostically restricted sample. The four clinical domains showed high reliability and generally acceptable discriminant validity. Family dysfunction was associated with maladaptive parenting and childhood trauma, and maladaptive parenting was associated with childhood trauma (β =0.384-0.600; all p <0.001). Childhood trauma was associated with greater rumination (β =0.625) and lower psychological resilience (β = -0.405; both p <0.001). Rumination and psychological resilience showed opposing associations with all four domains (rumination: β =0.280-0.559; resilience: β = -0.399 to -0.213; all p ≤.026). Family dysfunction, maladaptive parenting, and childhood trauma showed significant total indirect associations with all four domains (all p <0.001). The model explained 52-85% of variance across the four domains. Adolescent psychopathology was multidimensional, with related but distinguishable clinical domains sharing several psychosocial and cognitive-emotional correlates. The findings support examining domain-level psychopathology rather than relying exclusively on categorical diagnostic status and global depression severity.

abstract: Social media can foster engagement and sharing across community networks. Despite such utility, community health workers (CHWs) and community leaders have used social media inconsistently as part of their public health outreach activities, potentially limiting the promotion of community projects and hindering partnership development. The objectives of this mixed methods study were to (1) explore CHWs' and community leaders' experiences with and preferences for communication tools to address community needs and (2) describe the development of their social media capacity, including Facebook page and post analytics, as well as post content. From August to September 2022, we conducted a needs assessment using semistructured interviews with a purposive sample of CHWs and community leaders belonging to local health equity action teams (LHEATs) in 20 Kansas counties participating in a community-academic partnership. The complete interview dataset was analyzed with a phenomenological approach combined with a hybrid deductive and inductive analysis. We extracted from the dataset 2 communication-related questions to explore factors that eased or impeded LHEATs' promotional activities. Simultaneously, the academic team began assisting LHEATs in establishing Facebook pages and provided 3 trainings on the use of social media. We summarized quantitative data on page- and post-level Facebook analytics from organic and paid posts. We assessed the content of a simple random sample of 10% of the organic and paid LHEAT posts over a 3-year period from May 2022 to May 2025. Three themes emerged from 91 interviews: (1) LHEATs blended traditional channels (face-to-face, radio, and local newspapers) with social media, with Facebook being the most used; (2) leaders leveraged personal networks to amplify messages; and (3) participants sought clear separation between personal and professional accounts and audiences. Of the 20 LHEATs, 12 (60%) established Facebook pages and amassed 1732 followers. A total of 999 organic and paid posts were created during the 3-year period; they generated 158,697 unique users who saw the LHEATs' content (reach), 205,854 impressions, 8978 engagements, and 11,422 clicks. Notably, 20% (31,135/158,697) of the reach and 29.2% (60,021/205,854) of the impressions were from a paid Medicaid re-enrollment campaign. Post content mostly addressed community cohesion and access to resources (eg, health, community, and housing). Integrating social media into a statewide community-academic partnership is feasible. Academic partners can provide capacity training to facilitate and support LHEATs in leading, managing, and creating Facebook content that reflects community priorities. Paid social media has the potential to accelerate this outreach. Such equity-oriented communication efforts may have the potential to lay the groundwork for future health equity work.

abstract: Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the associations between socio-emotional competence and self-reported academic achievement among Grade 4 and Grade 5 students in public primary schools in Yunnan Province, China. Specifically, it investigates four dimensions of socio-emotional competence: self-management, social awareness, prosocial behavior, and learning attitude. It also examines whether the teacher-student relationship functions as an indirect pathway between socio-emotional competence and self-reported academic achievement. A cross-sectional quantitative design was adopted, and data were collected from 314 primary school students. Structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed relationships. The findings show that social awareness and prosocial behavior were positively associated with self-reported academic achievement, whereas self-management was not statistically significant. Learning attitude showed a statistically significant but unexpected negative association, suggesting the need for further investigation in high-pressure educational contexts. The teacher-student relationship did not function as a statistically significant indirect pathway between socio-emotional competence and self-reported academic achievement (z = 1.13, p = 0.249). These findings provide preliminary evidence that specific dimensions of socio-emotional competence may relate differently to academic outcomes in Chinese primary education. However, the results should be interpreted cautiously because of the cross-sectional design, reliance on self-reported academic achievement, partial model fit, and discriminant validity concerns among several constructs. The study contributes to context-sensitive discussions of socio-emotional competence in non-Western primary education settings and highlights the need for culturally grounded approaches to socio-emotional development in Chinese schools.

abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

abstract: Mosques play a vital role in Islam, serving not only as places of worship but also as centers for various social activities and economic empowerment, including the collection of social funds such as zakat, infaq, and sadaqah (charity). However, data from the 2024 Mosque Information System (SIMAS) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shows that of the total 694,725 mosques and prayer rooms, only 28,138 have a Mosque Welfare Agency (BKM), indicating that the majority of mosque management remains traditional and has not adopted modern management. Masjid Raya Al Insan (MRAI) in Kebayoran Lama, South Jakarta, is known for frequently holding social and humanitarian activities, both routine and incidental, for the congregation and the community living around the mosque. Previous research has examined factors such as transparency, accountability, the attitude of mosque management, and the social and religious influences of donors on trust and donation decisions. However, there is still little research that specifically examines the role of the effectiveness of mosque social activities and their consistency on repeat donation decisions. Using a qualitative case study method through in-depth interviews with administrators and donors, this study evaluates the role of the effectiveness and consistency of MRAI's social programs on repeat donations. The results show that the effectiveness of social activities is assessed by the emotional impact and tangible solutions for the community, not simply by statistical figures. It was found that repeat donation decisions are driven by a strong synergy between theological motivation and trust in the integrity of the administrators. Specifically, the consistency of social programs proved to be a key factor in building donor loyalty, validating the paradigm that "busy mosques" that actively distribute funds actually attract more donations. The study concluded that program consistency creates a sense of security and inner satisfaction for donors. As a recommendation, mosque administrators need to immediately undertake digital transformation in transparent financial reporting and implement Customer Relationship Management (CRM) to maintain donor relationships to ensure the sustainability of funding for community programs.

abstract: This study examines differential effects that different demographic variables and the subgroup-based community management model in universities on college students' prosocial behavior. abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is often paroxysmal and asymptomatic, yet early identification could enable targeted surveillance. Deep learning can predict future AF from a single 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), but AF develops through progressive atrial remodeling. We hypothesized that modeling each patient's longitudinal ECG history would improve 1-year AF prediction over a matched single-ECG model. We developed a transformer-based model that accepts variable-length sequences of prior 12-lead ECGs with time-aware encoding of irregular intervals. We compared it with a single-ECG model sharing the same encoder, covariates, preprocessing, outcome definition, and splits. Models were developed at Weill Cornell Medicine/NewYork-Presbyterian and evaluated on MIMIC-IV-ECG without and with fine-tuning. The outcome was AF documented more than 1 and within 365 days after an index ECG. Discrimination used patient-cluster bootstrapping with 1 random index ECG per patient. Cohorts included 107,811 institutional and 55,307 MIMIC-IV-ECG patients. The fine-tuned longitudinal model with age and sex discriminated best (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve: 0.85; C-index 0.84), exceeding the single-ECG model with age and sex (paired area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve: +0.007; 95% CI: 0.003-0.012; +0.014 with ≥1 prior ECG). Without retraining on MIMIC-IV-ECG, the ECG-only advantage was confined to patients with ≥1 prior ECG (+0.014; 95% CI: 0.004-0.024). After external-domain adaptation, the matched advantage was +0.007 (95% CI: 0.002-0.012). High-risk patients had lower AF-free survival (HR: 8.8; 95% CI: 7.8-10.0). A longitudinal deep learning model using serial 12-lead ECGs improved 1-year AF prediction over a matched single-ECG model. Longitudinal ECG modeling may provide a scalable approach to identify patients warranting enhanced AF surveillance.

abstract: Avatars serve as virtual representations of users in digital environments. Their appearance can be freely customized, often leading to discrepancies between visual representation and the user's real identity. Such appearances may unconsciously influence interpersonal trust, complicating the assessment of trustworthiness in virtual interactions. To investigate how avatar characteristics influence trust, we developed and preliminarily validated the Avatar Trust Scale (ATS), a tool designed to quantify trust specifically in the context of avatars. Based on data from a German sample of 840 participants, our findings suggest a two-factor structure: Specific Trust (trustworthiness, security, and willingness to interact) and General Trust (propensity to trust avatars and humans, and avatar literacy). The scale was validated using questionnaire data and behavioral tasks (i.e., trust game, dictator game, ultimatum game). Participants interacted with a virtual agent rather than a user-controlled avatar, providing initial validation in a controlled context and laying the groundwork for future research on avatar-mediated trust.

abstract: Conventional demographic models systematically overestimate fertility decline in sub-Saharan Africa. This paper proposes a complementary explanation grounded in a prevalent but understudied belief system: ancestors influence the living and seek the continuation of their lineage. In this worldview, having children becomes a moral and collective duty, rooted in the spiritual responsibility to ensure the survival of the lineage. Drawing on first-hand data, novel ethnographic information, and historical and contemporary surveys, I document a strong and quantitatively large positive relationship between ancestral beliefs and fertility across contexts and time periods. A simple model in which children are a public good for the lineage rationalizes the patterns observed in the data: the fertility effect of ancestral beliefs is concentrated in patrilineal societies, and a specific form of free-riding emerges among siblings whose children continue the same family line. • Beliefs in ancestral spirits raise fertility across sub-Saharan Africa. • Shown in Benin, the DR Congo, 19 countries today, and global folklore records. • Having children is a collective duty to the lineage, not a private choice. • Effects concentrate in patrilineal societies, where sons continue the line. • Free-riding appears among siblings whose children continue the same line.

abstract: Do young infants expect people to help one another? In two experiments (N = 72), the present study examined 5.5-month-old infants’ helping expectations as they watched two female agents’ actions. After seeing one agent try but fail to obtain an out-of-reach toy and then exit, infants expected another agent to help by moving the toy within her reach and found it unexpected when the agent did not. Importantly, if the first agent did not try to reach for the toy, signaling no need for it, infants instead found it unexpected when the other agent helped. Together, these results suggest that infants at this young age already expect people to be helpful toward others in need. These findings thus shed new light on the early development of moral cognition.

abstract: This paper contributes to debates on problematic, dominant criminological narratives by foregrounding children’s own accounts of the support they need to thrive, informing ongoing efforts to support their individual and moral development. Drawing on community-based, participatory focus groups and individual and small-group interviews with 58 children aged 10–17 attending youth centres in Cambridge (UK), the study departs from deficit-oriented, adult-led explanations that frame children primarily through risk, mental disorders, or criminalisation. The findings rework prevailing criminological intervention approaches in two ways. First, using reflexive thematic analysis, the study centres children’s lived knowledge to identify trust, belonging, voice, agency, relational consistency of care, emotional support, and autonomy as central to what makes interventions trustworthy, accessible, engaging, and effective, whilst overly didactic, rigid, or authoritarian approaches were identified as key barriers to participation and effectiveness. These accounts move beyond adult assumptions about children’s needs, showing that effective support is grounded in relational, dialogic, autonomy-supportive environments rather than deficit-oriented models. Second, the paper argues that centring children’s perspectives is necessary but not sufficient: interventions must also be theoretically informed and evidence based. Rather than treating participatory and evidence-informed approaches as competing paradigms, the study offers data supporting their integration, combining child-centred qualitative insight with theoretically specified explanations of behaviour. Implications are discussed for the ongoing development of the school-based SATNAV:Compass youth intervention programme. This reconstruction of recommended intervention design approaches retains the strengths of existing traditions whilst addressing their limitations, offering a direction for future intervention research and practice.

abstract: Wearable sensor technologies are now widely adopted in professional sports for high-frequency health and performance monitoring during training and, in some cases, recovery periods, generating multimodal physiological and self-reported wellness data. These data carry high privacy sensitivity as protected personal health information, and in competitive sports they additionally hold tactical intelligence value. Consequently, multiorganization data sharing remains institutionally infeasible, creating data silos that constrain the scalability of data-driven health risk classification models. Federated learning (FL) has shown promise in health care for collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, but systematic empirical validation on athlete-level wearable health data with quantified, genuinely non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) characteristics-spanning label, quantity, and covariate shift-remains absent. The present study therefore aimed to determine whether FL can achieve training load risk classification performance equivalent to centralized training while keeping raw athlete health data on-device, and to systematically investigate the key factors affecting FL efficacy in heterogeneous wearable health data scenarios. The publicly available SoccerMon dataset was used, comprising daily monitoring records from 50 elite female football players (all released players retained; filtering applied at the record level only) across 2 independent teams over the 2020 and 2021 seasons (36,550 raw records). A 21-dimensional multimodal feature matrix was constructed from 7 training load metrics derived from session rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) and its exponentially weighted moving averages (including the acute: chronic workload ratio [ACWR]), 7 subjective wellness indicators, and 7 binary missingness indicators. Using 28-day sliding windows, the future 7-day mean ACWR was classified into 3 risk levels (19,421 supervised samples). The federated clients exhibited three concurrent non-IID characteristics: label-distribution skew (SD of the high-risk class proportion across athlete clients 9.4% in TeamA and 21.7% in TeamB), quantity skew (mean 267-313 training windows per client), and between-team covariate shift that was statistically significant on all key training-load indicators but small in magnitude (Mann-Whitney r = .034-0.104), indicating that client-level rather than team-level heterogeneity dominates. Two-layer stacked long short-term memory (LSTM) networks served as client models within FedAvg and FedProx frameworks, compared against a centralized LSTM and 5 traditional machine learning baselines across single-team (K = 27), cross-team (K = 49), and team-level (K = 2) federated scenarios. All core experiments were repeated 30 times with Bonferroni-corrected paired t tests and Cohen d effect sizes. Team-level FedAvg retained 94.1% of centralized κ (0.401, SD 0.023 vs. 0.426, SD 0.018); cross-team athlete-level FedAvg retained 92.0% (κ = 0.392, SD 0.019); and single-team FedAvg retained 90.0% (κ = 0.366, SD 0.021). Two one-sided tests (TOST) established equivalence within a ± 0.05 κ practical bound between FL and centralized training in the cross-team and team-level scenarios (both TOST P ≤ .001), and between FedAvg and FedProx in all three scenarios (all TOST P < .001). High-risk recall remained within a narrow band across scenarios (FedAvg 0.767-0.828 vs. centralized LSTM 0.796-0.806). A naive persistence baseline reached κ of only 0.253-0.262, exceeded by FedAvg by 44.6%-53.1%, indicating that the model captures substantial structure beyond trivial autoregression. FedAvg and FedProx performed equivalently, with FedAvg approximately twice as computationally efficient. Load-only training features (7 dimensions) matched the full 21-dimensional set, and sRPE-derived internal load features contributed the majority of predictive importance. FL enables training load risk classification statistically equivalent to centralized training within a ± 0.05 κ practical bound, without sharing raw wearable health data, providing a viable privacy-preserving pathway for cross-organization sports analytics and health monitoring collaboration. These findings extend FL validation from clinical health care to athlete-level wearable health data with genuine non-IID characteristics, and remain robust under strictly causal data preprocessing.

abstract: Personality prompts reshape how Large Language Models propose offers in economic games—but not how they respond to them. We show this by assigning graded Dark Factor of Personality profiles to 17 LLMs in the Ultimatum Game and benchmarking their decisions against human data. As proposers, LLMs shifted from 91% fair offers at the lowest selfishness level to 17% at the highest, closely tracking human patterns but with steeper gradients. As responders, no such shift occurred: acceptance rates remained uniformly high ( ∼ 80%) regardless of personality, failing to reproduce the punishment dynamics observed in humans. This asymmetry is theoretically informative. When incentive structures are explicit, personality and framing effects are attenuated—and proposing an offer is inherently more ambiguous than responding to one.. Most strikingly, personality prompts changed what responders articulated but not how they chose : model justifications showed systematic shifts in fairness language, yet behavioral output remained flat. This dissociation between stated reasoning and revealed behavior indicates that LLMs achieve linguistic compliance with personality prompts without corresponding motivational change—approximating human strategic behavior only where surface-level heuristics suffice.

abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.
